P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. As an EU member state, Croatia applies Article 63 TFEU, which prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments between EU countries and with non-EU countries. Banks still apply AML/KYC checks and may ask for the source of funds.

sources.title: Free movement of capital (European Parliament Fact Sheet)
sources.quote: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and payments between EU countries, as well as between EU and non-EU countries.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Very likely yes: Article 63 TFEU removes capital-movement restrictions, and EU banks and e-money institutions commonly offer foreign-currency or multi-currency accounts. No Croatia-specific source on account rules was captured.
P2_fcy_account.note: Only the general EU capital-movement source captured; no national bank/regulator source on FCY accounts (2026-10-23).

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Freelancers usually trade as an obrt (sole proprietorship), registered with the local administrative office or online via e-Obrt. Within 8 days of receiving the decision on entry in the Craft Register (Obrtni registar), you must report to the competent Tax Administration (Porezna uprava) office to enter the taxpayer register (form RPO) and choose a taxation method: flat-rate paušalni, or bookkeeping. You also need an OIB (personal tax number) and registration with the pension (HZMO) and health (HZZO) insurers. Some liberal professions (e.g. health workers, vets, athletes, lawyers) cannot use flat-rate taxation.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: National threshold: EUR 60,000 of annual receipts is the amount that triggers mandatory entry into the VAT system, and the same figure caps the flat-rate paušalni regime. Crossing it ends paušalni taxation (see L7). The standard VAT rate is 25%. Under the EU SME scheme, small businesses below a national threshold (at most EUR 85,000) can be exempt on domestic sales. Where services are taxed (EU-wide rules, illustrated by Irish Revenue guidance): (1) B2B, meaning services to business customers in other EU countries or outside the EU, are taxed where the customer is established, so no Croatia VAT is charged; EU business customers self-account under the reverse charge. (2) B2C services to private individuals are, as a rule, taxed where the supplier is established, so Croatia VAT applies once you are VAT-registered. (3) Exception: consultancy, legal, accounting, engineering, data-processing, advertising, licensing and electronically supplied services to private customers outside the EU are outside EU VAT, subject to 'use and enjoyment' rules. Electronically supplied services to private customers in other EU countries follow special OSS rules (not captured here).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies directly in Croatia, supervised by the national data protection authority. It covers EU businesses and non-EU businesses offering goods or services to people in the EU.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: EU consumer law gives a 14-day withdrawal right for online and distance purchases without justification: 14 days from delivery for goods, and from conclusion of the contract for services. Exceptions include personalised goods, perishables and date-specific services.

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: For goods this means 14 days from the date of delivery, for services 14 days after the day the contract was agreed.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: Paušalni obrt (flat-rate craft): available to any craft activity, regardless of number of employees, provided you are not VAT-registered and annual receipts do not exceed EUR 60,000 (liberal professions excluded, see L1). Income tax is a fixed amount by receipt class: 12% of a deemed base, paid quarterly by the last day of each quarter. 2026 classes run from EUR 203.40 a year (receipts up to EUR 11,300) to EUR 1,080 a year (EUR 50,000.01–60,000). Pension and health contributions are separate fixed monthly amounts (2026 figures differ between sources). TRAP, changes for 2027: the government announced that totals stay unchanged for receipts up to EUR 40,000 (about 83% of flat-rate traders). For the 6th class, total annual tax plus contributions rise by EUR 1,336 to EUR 5,728; for the top class (EUR 50,000.01–60,000), by EUR 3,033 to EUR 7,605. Fiskalopedija's 2027 table puts the top-class tax alone at EUR 3,240 a year.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
